title: elif versus separate ifs
idea: A chain picks one winner; separate ifs can each fire. See why that difference matters for classifying. Thinking-heavy.

exercises.explanation: These are TWO separate ifs, so both tests run. 95 passes both, printing two lines - often not what you want.
elif chains them: the first match (A) wins and the elif is skipped. Exactly one line prints.

exercises.prompt: Separate ifs each test independently, so more than one can run.
exercises.explanation: Yes - without elif, each if is its own decision and any number of them can fire.

exercises.prompt: An if/elif chain lets at most one branch run.
exercises.explanation: Right - a chain stops at the first True, so exactly one (or zero, if no else) branch runs.

exercises.prompt: You want to put a score into ONE grade bucket. Which structure is correct?
exercises.explanation: A single bucket means one winner - that is exactly what an if/elif/else chain guarantees.

exercises.prompt: When might separate ifs be the RIGHT choice?
options: When several independent things can each be true at once
exercises.explanation: If conditions are independent (e.g. 'has coupon' and 'is member'), separate ifs let each act on its own.

exercises.prompt: A bug: a grade program prints both 'B' and 'A' for a 95. Likely cause?
options: Two separate ifs were used instead of an elif chain
exercises.explanation: Separate ifs both fired. Chaining them with elif makes only the first match print.

exercises.prompt: Arrange a correct one-winner chain for 90/80/else.
exercises.explanation: if then elif then else makes exactly one grade print. That is the fix for the double-print bug.

exercises.prompt:
Change the second if into a chained branch:

if score >= 90:
    print("A")
____ score >= 80:
    print("B")
exercises.explanation: Replacing the second 'if' with 'elif' links the tests so only the first match prints.

options: elif = one winner; separate ifs = each can fire
exercises.explanation: Pick a chain when exactly one outcome should win; pick separate ifs when truly independent things can each happen.
